Question nine. Why fix the sample size in advance instead of peeking? Here both arms are identical, and the p-value is recomputed every hundred visitors. It dips under point oh five at eight hundred, and again at two thousand. Stop at either, and you've shipped noise. At the planned eight thousand, it's point one nine. Run ten thousand of these A A tests. Checked once, at the end, four point nine percent come out significant. Checked weekly, twelve. Daily for four weeks, twenty-six and a half. Every hundred visitors, thirty-five.

Question ten. What is a sequential probability ratio test? An S P R T tracks the likelihood ratio between two hypotheses, no effect and the effect you designed for, against boundaries fixed before the start. Cross the top line, and you conclude there's an effect. Cross the bottom, and there isn't. In between, you keep going. Run it two thousand times each way. It wrongly finds an effect two percent of the time, within the two and a half it was built for. And when the effect is real, it stops after two hundred sixty-two pairs of users on average, against three hundred ninety-three for the fixed test. One more choice makes every test cheaper to run.

Question eleven. What is CUPED, and how does it reduce variance? It stands for Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data. What a user did before the test predicts a lot of what they do during it. So subtract the part the pre-period predicts: theta times the user's distance from the average. On the page's five hundred users, the variance falls from eight point oh nine to three point five two. The average stays exactly where it was. Only the noise shrinks, so the same power needs less than half the users.
